summary: This RFC extends IKEv2 for group key management, following the MSEC architecture with member registration and group rekeying. It obsoletes RFC 6407.

eli5.summary: A group needs one shared secret and a way to change it when people leave. This uses IKEv2 to hand it out.

questions: how does ipsec multicast group key management work
subtitle: How IKEv2 is stretched to hand keys and policy to a whole IPsec multicast group, and to change them later.

tldr.problem: IPsec devices that talk to a whole group, such as over IP multicast, all need the same Security Associations and keys, and someone has to hand them out and renew them.
tldr.mechanism: G-IKEv2 extends IKEv2 with new exchanges. A Group Member registers with a Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS), which authorizes it and downloads policy and wrapped keys. The GCKS later rekeys the group, either by one multicast message or by a unicast exchange with each member.
tldr.outcome: G-IKEv2 replaces the IKEv1-based Group Domain of Interpretation (RFC 6407), which it obsoletes.

today: RFC 9838 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2025. It obsoletes RFC 6407, the IKEv1-based Group Domain of Interpretation, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Group Key Management
sections.content:
RFC 9838 defines G-IKEv2, an extension to IKEv2 for group key management. A group key management protocol gives IPsec keys and policy to a set of IPsec devices that are allowed to communicate using a Group Security Association (GSA). Group traffic, such as IP multicast packets, is protected by a key that the Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS) pushes to the Group Members (GMs).

G-IKEv2 has two phases: registration, where a GM contacts the GCKS and receives policy and keys, and rekeying, where the GCKS renews keying material for GM-to-GM traffic and for GM-to-GCKS traffic. It conforms to the MSEC architecture documents and replaces the Group Domain of Interpretation in RFC 6407, which used IKEv1.

The RFC also defines the terms it uses. A TEK is the traffic encryption key of a Data-Security SA, which carries group data from senders to receivers. A KEK protects the messages of the Rekey SA, a single multicast SA from the GCKS to all GMs. A KWK is a key used to protect another key.
sections.eli5: A group of friends wants to pass secret notes. One friend is the key keeper who decides who is in and hands out the secret code, and the others use that code to write to each other.

sections.title: Registering a Group Member
sections.content:
Registration begins with the normal IKE_SA_INIT exchange from IKEv2, which negotiates algorithms, swaps nonces and computes a shared key. In G-IKEv2 it also negotiates a key wrap algorithm through a new Key Wrap Algorithm transform. The second exchange is GSA_AUTH, which is like IKE_AUTH but has its own exchange type. The GM sends its identity, authentication and an IDg payload naming the group it wants to join. The GCKS authenticates and authorizes it, then answers with a GSA payload (policy) and a KD payload (keys).

The GM may add an SAg payload listing the transforms it is willing to accept. Policy is not negotiated; the SAg only tells the GCKS about the GM's limits. A GM that wants to send data MUST include a GROUP_SENDER notification. Including SAg is RECOMMENDED.

Once the IKE SA exists, a GM can register to further groups with the GSA_REGISTRATION exchange. Failures come back as notifications such as INVALID_GROUP_ID, AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, REGISTRATION_FAILED or NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN. A GM that finds the policy unacceptable SHOULD tell the GCKS with a GSA_REGISTRATION exchange, and then the GCKS MUST remove it from the group.

A GM installs a Data-Security SA only inbound if it is not a sender, and a Rekey SA only inbound. By convention the GCKS closes the registration IKE SA, though it MAY keep it open for in-band rekey, especially in small groups. If the SA is closed and no rekey policy was received, the GM must consider itself excluded and re-register.
sections.eli5: To join, you knock on the key keeper's door and say which club you want. They check your ID, and if you are allowed in they give you the club's rules and a secret key.

sections.title: Rekeying the Group
sections.content:
The GCKS rekeys when membership or policy changes or when keys are about to expire. Two channels exist. GSA_REKEY is a pseudo-exchange: a single one-way message, usually sent over IP multicast, which suits large and dynamic groups. GSA_INBAND_REKEY is a normal IKEv2 exchange over the registration IKE SA, which delivers policy reliably and suits small groups. A GCKS MAY combine them, for example in-band for senders and multicast for the rest.

A GSA_REKEY message carries GSA and KD payloads, and optionally an AUTH payload. Its Message ID rises with every message, and a GM rejects any message whose Message ID is smaller than expected, which gives replay protection. Because multicast rekeys are not acknowledged, the GCKS may send several bitwise identical copies a few seconds apart. The AUTH payload MUST be included when authentication is by public-key signature and MUST NOT be included for implicit authentication. Implicit authentication, which only proves the sender knows the current KEK, is NOT RECOMMENDED except for small groups of highly trusted members.

To remove SAs, the GCKS sends a Delete payload. An SPI of zero with Protocol ID GIKE_UPDATE tells a GM that it has been excluded; it must re-register if it wants back in, and it is RECOMMENDED to wait a random time first to avoid overloading the GCKS.
sections.eli5: When the secret code has to change, the key keeper either shouts the new code through a megaphone to everyone, or quietly tells each person one at a time. The megaphone is quick for a crowd, and the whisper is safer for a few friends.

sections.title: Counter Modes, Sender-IDs and Replay Protection
sections.content:
Counter-based ciphers such as AES-GCM require that no two senders ever use the same IV with the same key. G-IKEv2 meets this by giving each Data-Security SA its own key and by using the method of RFC 6054: the GCKS gives every sender a unique Sender-ID, which fills the most significant bits of the IV. The GWP_SENDER_ID_BITS attribute says how many bits that is.

The GCKS allocates Sender-IDs from a counter, starting at zero, and hands out new ones on every registration by a sender. When the counter runs out, the GCKS MUST exclude all GMs before issuing more, which forces re-registration and fresh Data-Security SAs.

Replay protection is limited. If many senders share an SA, each increments the ESP sequence number independently, so receivers cannot filter replays. With only one sender it is possible, and then the GCKS MUST rekey often enough that the 32-bit sequence numbers do not wrap. A new Sequence Numbers transform, "32-bit Unspecified Numbers", tells GMs that sequence numbers are not guaranteed unique. Encryption transforms with implicit IV rely on unique sequence numbers, so they MUST NOT be used unless that holds, and MUST NOT be used for any G-IKEv2 SA.
sections.eli5: If everyone numbers their notes starting from one, the numbers clash. So the key keeper gives each writer their own range of numbers, and no two notes ever get the same number.

sections.title: Key Wrapping and Access Control
sections.content:
Keys are never sent in clear. Every key the GCKS sends is encrypted by another key, called a Key Wrap Key (KWK). Every GM knows at least the default KWK, GSK_w. For the unicast IKE SA it is computed as prf+(SK_d, "Key Wrap for G-IKEv2"); for the multicast Rekey SA it comes with the SA keys.

The GCKS chooses how elaborate key management is. A simple method always wraps group SA keys with GSK_w. The Logical Key Hierarchy (LKH) method gives each GM a personal key and builds a tree, so that group keys are wrapped under keys wrapped under keys, back to each member. This allows forward access control, meaning a removed member cannot get new keys, and backward access control, meaning a new member cannot get old ones. A GM that cannot build a key path to the new key knows it has been excluded.

To keep policy hidden from an excluded member, the GCKS MUST send two sequential rekey messages. The first creates a new KEK, and the second carries the changed policy and TEKs, protected under the new KEK. A rekey message MUST NOT change policy without creating a new KEK. Appendix A shows LKH in detail.
sections.eli5: It is like keeping a small key in a box, then that box in a bigger box, and so on. Kicking someone out just means changing the locks they never had keys for.

sections.title: New Payloads and Exchange Types
sections.content:
G-IKEv2 keeps the IKEv2 header with Major Version 2 and Minor Version 0, and adds the exchange types GSA_AUTH, GSA_REGISTRATION, GSA_REKEY and GSA_INBAND_REKEY. It adds four payloads: IDg (Group Identification, payload type 50), SAg (GM Supported Transforms, type 33, the same as the SA payload), GSA (Group Security Association, type 51) and KD (Key Download, type 52).

The GSA payload holds group policies of two kinds: group SA policy, built from transforms, and group-wide (GW) policy, such as the Activation and Deactivation Time Delays that smooth key rollover. Two new transform types are defined: Group Controller Authentication Method (GCAUTH, type 14), whose values are Implicit and Digital Signature, and Key Wrap Algorithm.

The KD payload carries key bags. A Group Key Bag holds keying material for one SA, while a Member Key Bag (first byte zero) holds a single member's keys, such as WRAP_KEY, AUTH_KEY and GM_SENDER_ID. Wrapped keys have a 4-octet Key ID, a 4-octet KWK ID and the encrypted key. G-IKEv2 can use the IKEv2 ports 500 and 4500, TCP encapsulation, or UDP port 848 as GDOI does; the version number in the IKE header tells the two apart.
sections.eli5: The messages are like forms. G-IKEv2 adds a few new forms: one to say which club you want, one for the rules, and one for the keys.

sections.title: Working with Other IKEv2 and ESP Extensions
sections.content:
G-IKEv2 is compatible with most IKEv2 extensions. EAP authentication, EAP-only authentication, secure password authentication, the redirect mechanism, session resumption, IKE_INTERMEDIATE and multiple key exchanges are all named as usable. Some need special handling.

Implicit IV, which depends on unique ESP sequence numbers, cannot be used on multi-sender multicast SAs but can be used with a single sender. Aggregation and fragmentation mode for ESP likewise needs a single-sender SA in tunnel mode and cannot use its congestion control feature. Post-quantum preshared keys (RFC 8784) protect the group keys, since GSK_w derives from SK_d. Other data sent over the initial IKE SA stays exposed, so a GCKS that cares MUST use an extension that protects the initial IKE SA too.

Extensions that were defined for GDOI are expected to be redefined for G-IKEv2 in separate documents if needed.
sections.eli5: The new system plays nicely with most of the older add-ons, but a few add-ons only work when there is just one speaker.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A joining entity has to trust that the GCKS only admits authorized entities and that other members will not leak what the group shares. Registration inherits the IKEv2 protections for authentication, confidentiality, on-path attack protection, replay and reflection protection, and denial-of-service protection. G-IKEv2 also lets the GCKS authorize a particular member whether or not it holds IKEv2 credentials.

The maintenance channel is protected with the algorithms and keys negotiated at registration. Rekey messages are authenticated with the distributed authentication key, or only implicitly, which proves group membership but not that the GCKS sent the message. A Message ID that is less than or equal to the last received value MUST be discarded. Because a Rekey SA is inbound only for GMs, reflection is prevented.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to trust the key keeper to let in only the right people, and trust the other members to keep the secret.
